passage:
Tuesday. Yash saw Gurleen, the senior quality lead, open last month’s inspection file after office hours. A line about a failed check now read “passed.” Yash said nothing and went back to his desk.
Thursday. The team met behind closed doors twice. When Yash went in for coffee, the talk stopped. Everyone studied their cups, and nobody looked at anyone.
Monday. Yash had spent the weekend unsure. Then he wrote down the dates and the file name and asked the compliance officer for a private talk. He kept to facts. “I may be wrong,” he said, “but I want it looked at.” The officer listened, thanked him and said the file would be checked. In the corridor Gurleen passed him and didn’t meet his eyes.

qa.q: What had changed in the inspection file that Yash saw on Tuesday?
qa.a: A line about a failed check now read “passed.”

qa.q: What was Yash feeling over the weekend before he asked for a private talk?
qa.a: Yash was unsure and uneasy, weighing whether he had seen correctly and what speaking up might cost. His careful notes and his words, I may be wrong, show doubt alongside a wish to act.

qa.q: What made Yash's approach to the compliance officer sensible?
qa.a: Yash wrote down dates and the file name, kept to facts and admitted he might be wrong. That gave the compliance officer something checkable rather than an accusation.

qa.q: What might Gurleen have been feeling when passing Yash without meeting his eyes?
qa.a: Gurleen may have felt uneasy or guilty, or simply awkward at the silence in the team. The passage does not say what Gurleen knew, so this is a guess.

grounding: Shows a team member noticing altered documents and closed-door meetings and deciding whom to tell.

passage:
Bhavna, sit down. When I was a junior clerk at a bank branch, I noticed a clerk correcting ledger pages after the auditors’ call. I’m Uday, and I was twenty-four then. The manager shut his door. The tea boy stopped his rounds. Nobody in the room spoke, and Mr. Sinha, the old cashier, kept looking at his hands.
That night I did not sleep. Next morning I wrote down dates and page numbers and went to the audit head. I said, “I saw pages corrected after the call. I don’t know why.”
Weeks later Mr. Sinha told me he’d been waiting for someone younger to speak first.

qa.q: What did Uday notice after the auditors' call?
qa.a: Uday noticed a clerk correcting ledger pages after the auditors' call.

qa.q: What might Mr. Sinha have been feeling as he kept looking at his hands?
qa.a: Mr. Sinha may have felt uneasy and afraid for his position, and unwilling to be the first to speak. His words weeks later, that he was waiting for someone younger, suggest it weighed on him.

qa.q: Which choice did Uday make the next morning, and why was it careful?
qa.a: Uday wrote down dates and page numbers and went to the audit head, saying what was seen and admitting not knowing why. That gave facts without accusation.

qa.q: What might the manager have felt when shutting his door?
qa.a: The manager was probably worried about the branch being found out and wanted to avoid being overheard. The passage shows only the closed door.

grounding: An elder recalls watching pages quietly altered at a bank branch, the silent room, and choosing to speak to the audit head.

passage: The auditors were due at nine the next morning, and a power cut had left the office running on the generator, lights flickering. Shalini, working late on the ledgers, watched through the glass as Suraj, the finance manager, and two directors closed the conference-room blinds. An hour later Suraj came out and asked her to 'replace' the October vendor file with a new version he had emailed. The new file showed payments to a company she had never heard of, dated weeks earlier. In the morning meeting, when the auditor asked about October, the room went silent. Suraj looked at the table. Shalini felt her heartbeat in her ears. She said nothing then. But at lunch she printed both versions of the file, put them in an envelope, and looked up the email address of the company's audit committee chair.

qa.q: Which file did Suraj ask Shalini to replace?
qa.a: The October vendor file.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when the room went silent?
qa.a: Her heartbeat was in her ears; she felt frightened and tense, knowing the file had been changed.

qa.q: What careful steps did Shalini take after the meeting?
qa.a: She printed both versions of the file, kept them safe, and looked up the audit committee chair so she could report to the right person.

qa.q: How might Suraj be feeling as he looks at the table?
qa.a: Probably tense and uneasy, perhaps guilty or afraid of being found out.

grounding: A colleague sees documents quietly changed and closed-door meetings, notices the silence and decides whom to tell.

passage: In the Hyderabad office of a logistics company, Suraj noticed things change after the warehouse accident. The first incident report, written by his colleague Binita, said a worker was hurt because the forklift's brakes had been failing for weeks. By Friday, the report in the shared folder said 'worker error', and Binita's name had been removed. The managers met behind closed doors twice, and when Suraj walked past, the talk stopped. At the team meeting, the manager read out the new version. Everyone stared at their laptops. Binita's face was blank. Suraj felt sick. Afterwards he found Binita at the water cooler. 'You wrote the first one, didn't you?' She nodded, eyes wet. 'I kept a copy.' That evening Suraj tagged the forklift DO NOT USE, and they agreed to take the copy together to the safety officer first thing in the morning.

qa.q: What did the report in the shared folder say by Friday?
qa.a: 'Worker error'.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel as everyone stared at their laptops?
qa.a: He felt sick and uneasy, noticing the silence and knowing the report had been changed.

qa.q: What did Suraj and Binita do, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Suraj tagged the forklift DO NOT USE that evening, and they agreed to take Binita's original copy together to the safety officer, a proper channel with evidence and support.

qa.q: What might Binita have been feeling during the meeting?
qa.a: Hurt and powerless, her blank face hiding distress as her report was rewritten and her name removed.

grounding: A colleague notices a report quietly rewritten after an accident and the silence in the room, and decides with a co-worker whom to tell.

passage:
'Did you see Tuesday's minutes?' Arohi whispered, closing the staffroom door.
Avni looked up. 'The trip meeting? Why?'
'The version on the drive says the bus had a "minor delay". I was there. The driver was on his phone and we nearly hit the divider. Two kids were hurt.'
Avni's face changed. 'Principal sir said we'd handle it quietly. For the school's name.'
'The parents weren't even told properly.' Arohi's hands were shaking. 'Everyone in that room just nodded.'
'Including us.'
Silence.
'So what do we do?' Avni asked. 'If we go to the principal again, he'll just—'
'Not him. The management committee, and the transport safety officer.' Arohi opened her laptop. 'I wrote down what I saw that day. Will you read it and add yours?'
Avni pulled her chair closer. 'Yes. And we call both families today.'

qa.q: What did the minutes on the drive say about the bus?
qa.a: That it had a 'minor delay'.

qa.q: What do Arohi's shaking hands show?
qa.a: Arohi is upset and anxious, disturbed by the cover-up and by everyone nodding along.

qa.q: What steps do Arohi and Avni plan, and why?
qa.a: Writing down what they saw, going to the management committee and transport safety officer instead of the principal, and calling both families today.

qa.q: How might the parents of the hurt children feel if they learn the truth later?
qa.a: Betrayed and angry that the school hid how their children were hurt.

grounding: Two colleagues notice meeting minutes quietly changed and the silence around an incident, and decide to speak to the right people.

passage: I'm Naveen, and for two weeks last autumn I watched our project office rewrite a report. It was the survey of how many families in the resettlement colony had actually received water connections. Our field numbers said 212 of 600. On Tuesday the draft on the shared drive said 480. The version history showed my manager's login at 11 p.m. Then the meetings started: the director, my manager and the donor liaison, door shut, blinds down. When they came out, nobody met anyone's eyes. At lunch Nazia, who had done half the field visits, asked quietly, "You saw it too?" I nodded. Nobody else said a word, and that silence was louder than any argument. That evening I kept my own copy of the field sheets and wrote down who might listen: the ethics officer, the donor's complaints desk. I haven't slept well since. On Monday I'm going with Nazia to the ethics officer.

qa.q: How many water connections did the field numbers show?
qa.a: The field numbers said 212 of 600.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling during the silence at lunch?
qa.a: Naveen felt uneasy and troubled; the silence seemed louder than any argument, and sleep has been poor ever since.

qa.q: What steps is Naveen taking, and why are they sensible?
qa.a: Keeping a copy of the field sheets, listing who might listen, and going with Nazia to the ethics officer uses a proper channel, with evidence and an ally.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel seeing the field work changed?
qa.a: Nazia likely feels hurt and alarmed, since half the visits were Nazia's, and is relieved to find someone else had noticed.

grounding: Naveen watches figures being quietly changed and closed-door meetings, notices the silence, and decides whom to tell.
